newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Officials probe Sao Paulo air disaster.
newsitem.headline: Officials probe Sao Paulo air disaster.

text.p: Federal authorities on Friday began probing what caused the crash of a Fokker-100 aircraft in a residential area of Sao Paulo that killed up to 104 people.

All 96 passengers and at least eight people on the ground died on Thursday when TAM airline flight 402 ploughed into the densely populated neighbourhood of Parque Jabaquara, just 30 seconds after take-off.

Officials at Brazil's Civil Aviation Department (DAC), which is responsible for investigating the accident, said they had recovered the Fokker's two black boxes, which contain recordings of the pilot's last conversation with his crew and with air controllers. They said a final report on the accident would be published within 90 days.

Eyewitnesses at Congonhas airport, the domestic flight terminal from which the 108-seat plane departed, said they saw the thrust reverter on the Fokker's right turbine deploy automatically as the plane raced down the runway.
The thrust reverter, which is used on landing to help bring a plane to a stop, is designed to reverse the direction of the engine's air intake creating an aerodynamic resistance.

Experts cited by Brazilian newspapers said that while the involuntary deployment of a thrust reverter was highly unusual, the effect of one of the plane's two engines pushing in the opposite direction could easily explain the crash.
"I saw the right engine's airbrake open up. That's not normal and creates a very strange sound," said Antonio Bueno, an aircraft mechanic at Congonhas airport.
"The next time I looked the plane took a dive and disappeared underneath a mushroom-shaped cloud," he said.
Firefighters who helped retrive the dead said the bent over position in which most of the victims were found suggested the passengers were aware of the imminent danger.
"Although the bodies were completely charred, one could see that they were bent over," Lieutenant Colonel Leopoldo Correa Filho said.
Officials said flight 402, which crashed less than a mile (1.6 km) from the end of the runway, never managed to climb above 90 feet (30 metres).
Sao Paulo morgue officials said they were having difficulty identifying the bodies because of the mutilated and burnt condition in which most had arrived.
By Friday morning only 24 of 97 bodies at the city morgue had been clearly identified, including those of an elderly woman who was travelling with her son and daughter.
TAM officials assembled family members of the victims at a hotel near Congonhas airport where they were shown videos of the victim's bodies so as to help speed up the identification process.
